summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Year 1): understand ADDITION as combining or putting together two groups to find the total ('how many altogether'). Teach both combining meanings explicitly — ADD-TO (a group grows: 3 here, 2 MORE arrive) and PUT-TOGETHER (two static parts seen as one whole). Keep the physical ACTION of joining visible before any written symbol, build on secure cardinality (last-number-said = how many), and attach the words 'altogether/total' to the whole combined set. Keep numbers small (within 5-10).
misconceptions: Recounting the whole from 1 every time and never trusting the total — a cardinality gap surfacing inside addition.
Thinking addition always means 'a group gets bigger by things arriving' (add-to only), so static put-together and part-part-whole situations aren't recognised as addition.
Believing the total is 'the last number you say' regardless of combining, i.e. reciting rather than combining quantities.
Losing track when combining by miscounting the join (double-counting an object or skipping one).
Assuming the bigger group must be said/written first, an early seed of not seeing addition as flexible (commutativity comes later).

activities.title: Combining mat: push two groups into one whole
steps: Drop three counters into one framed region (a basket or ten-frame) and two counters into a second framed region beside it.
Count each part aloud: 'three red here, two blue here.'
Physically sweep both piles together into a single large 'altogether' region.
Count the whole merged set and say how many there are altogether.
Say the matching sentence aloud: 'three and two more — that's five altogether.' (Leave the written 3 + 2 = 5 for the later, separate symbol topic.)
Switch modes: in ADD-TO, add objects to one existing group one at a time ('3... then 2 more arrive'); in PUT-TOGETHER, start with two ready-made parts and merge them at once.
activities.insight: Two separate groups the child made become ONE group with a single count — addition felt as a physical join, not a recited fact. 'Altogether' names the whole combined set, however it was built.

activities.title: Act out an add-to story
steps: Act out a situation with real children or toys: e.g. 3 children are on the mat, then 2 more join.
Narrate the action and the result separately: '3 children... then 2 more came... that's 5 altogether.'
State 'how many altogether' after the join without being told to recount from one.
Retell the story using fingers or a five-/ten-frame to show the growing group.
activities.insight: Add-to situations (a group grows as more arrive) are a form of addition, and the total names the whole group after the new members join.

activities.title: Part-part-whole picture scene and 'altogether?' flap
steps: Look at a static scene with two groups (e.g. 3 ducks on the bank, 2 ducks in the water).
Count each group by pointing to it.
Answer 'how many altogether?' and then check by lifting a flap or revealing the total.
Fit the two parts into a part-whole ('cherry') diagram: two parts joining into one whole.
activities.insight: Two static parts can be seen together as one whole — the put-together meaning of addition — even when nothing is moving or arriving.

activities.title: Talk it through while combining
steps: Alongside real objects, respond to a warm prompt: 'Let's put these together — how many now?'
Explain in words what 'altogether' means by showing it with the counters.
Answer probing questions: 'If I add the blue ones to the red ones instead of red to blue, do we still get 5? Why?' and 'What if there were 3 red and 4 blue — how many altogether?'
If a pretend friend says the answer is 3, explain what you would tell them.
activities.insight: A child can articulate that addition means combining to find how many altogether, and begins to notice the order of combining doesn't change the total.

checkQuestion: Here are 3 red counters and 2 blue counters. If I put them together, how many are there altogether? How did you work it out?
checkAnswer: 5 — found by combining the two groups into one, ideally counting ON from the larger group ('3 … 4, 5') or just knowing 3 and 2 make 5, rather than recounting every counter from one.
